hints: Count the alpha carbons in the diagram and look at what is attached to each one. You should see three residues with side chains H, CH(CH3)CH2CH3, and CH(CH3)2.
Remember what hydrolysis does to each -CO-NH- peptide bond. The C=O side gains OH to become COOH and the NH side gains H to become NH2.
walkthrough:
**Spot the three amino acid residues**

Look carefully at the chain. There are three central CH groups, each between a C=O and an NH. Their side chains are different.

Left residue has H and H, so R = H. Middle residue has R = CH(CH3)CH2CH3. Right residue has R = CH(CH3)2.

**Apply hydrolysis to the peptide bonds**

A peptide bond is -CO-NH-. Complete hydrolysis uses water to break it:
$$-CO-NH- + H_2O \rightarrow -COOH + H_2N-$$
So every free amino acid produced must have an amino end as $NH_2$ ($H_2N-CH-$) and an acid end as $COOH$ ($-C(=O)OH$). The R groups do not change.

**Match to the products**

We therefore expect three amino acids: glycine with R = H, plus the two branched-chain residues, all drawn as $H_2N-CH(R)-COOH$. Only option D shows all three with two H atoms on each N and OH on each C=O, with the correct R groups.

options.A: Shows the correct COOH ends and correct R groups, but each N is shown with only one H instead of NH2, so it cannot be the free amino acids from hydrolysis.
options.B: Shows NH2 correctly but the C ends are drawn as aldehydes with H instead of OH, so they are not carboxylic acids.
options.C: Shows NH2 correctly, but the middle amino acid has H on its carbonyl carbon instead of OH, so it is an aldehyde not an amino acid.
options.D: Shows all three residues with H2N- at the left, HOOC- at the right, and the correct R groups H, CH(CH3)CH2CH3 and CH(CH3)2.
